cases.answer: First, I take a full set of observations and compare them with the patient's last three sets in the electronic health record, so I can see the trend and not just the number. Then I do my hands-on assessment, listening to the chest, checking skin colour and capillary refill, and asking the patient how they feel in their own words. Finally, before I leave the bedside, I ask myself whether the story fits the numbers, and if it does not I repeat the reading with a different cuff or probe. On a night shift last month my own manual blood pressure looked too low for a patient who was chatting happily, so I rechecked it with the machine and found I had misplaced the cuff. This matters because a missed deterioration or a false alarm both land on the patient, who could be treated for the wrong problem or left too long.

cases.answer: I want to be a registered nurse because I was in hospital at sixteen with appendicitis and a night nurse sat with me for ten minutes explaining every step, which took away most of my fear. That stayed with me, and it is the kind of difference I want to make. My strengths are staying calm, noticing small changes and explaining things plainly, which fit the daily work of patient assessment, medication administration and care planning. As a healthcare assistant on a medical ward last year, I noticed a patient was more confused than usual at the morning round, reported it to the nurse in charge, and he turned out to have a urine infection that was treated that day. I know the role means more than tasks, it means being accountable for each patient's safety and coordinating with doctors and the wider team.

cases.answer: One strength is staying organised under pressure, and I showed it on a busy surgical ward when four patients came back from theatre within an hour. I was the nurse responsible for those four bays, so the order of care was my call. I did a quick airway and pain check on each of them, I listed who needed observations every fifteen minutes, and I asked the healthcare assistant to start the fluid balance charts. A second strength is communication, which I used when I explained a delayed discharge to an anxious family and wrote the plan on the whiteboard for them.

cases.answer: In the first two weeks I would read the last six months of patient survey comments and ask five patients on the ward what mattered most to them, so I know the real causes before changing anything. My measure would be the monthly question about feeling listened to, which sits at 71 percent today, and I would aim for 80 percent by day 90. Then, in weeks three to eight, I would try one free change at a time, such as a bedside whiteboard with the nurse's name and plan, and hourly comfort rounds. Finally, in the last month I would compare the scores and keep what worked. I would speak with the ward manager and doctors at the weekly huddle to share what patients said, and I would tell patients directly what we were changing and why.

cases.answer: First, I would let the new teammate watch me do two full patient assessments, explaining aloud what I check and why. Then they would do the same assessment on a stable patient, covering observations, skin, pain and the electronic health record entry, while I watch and stay quiet unless something is unsafe. Finally I would give feedback straight afterwards, ask them to repeat anything they missed, and sign them off only after three assessments that I have seen done correctly. This matters because a rushed assessment can miss a patient getting worse, and a new nurse who has not been shown properly can pass that habit on.
